human_labels.body: This is the main change in this PR besides reverting to https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/commit/d4ca814cbea037dcf2a59d083f8a540bf5d38d3a
We could be fancy and add some 🟢 green 🟢  here

Actually, I was being flippant here but it made me think about where we'd use red or yellow, and it made me think about having a generic failure message that reassures users that state is safe (not destroyed during migrate), the action can be retried multiple times, and some guidance on what to investigate (e.g do some ENVs need to be set).

I've now added `StateMigrationPostStepsInterruptedMessage` and `StateMigrationFailureMessage` with the main aims of:

- Notifying users when the failing command has definitely had effects on the destination location before erroring
- Reassuring users that the source state is not changed by Terraform and retrying is safe
- Directing users where to send bug reports to (migration errors may be due to providers, post-migration errors are due to Core).

I removed this bit because our argument parsing logic promises to make a "best effort" interpretation of args and flags, e.g. here for `plan`:

https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/e8f546c897a6db0cee23e96573c0622cf6bc4354/internal/command/arguments/plan.go#L41-L43

This looks like not returning early and instead returning errors alongside a representation of the args/flags.
We could probably remove use of the location data here?

Eh, looking at it further I think we want to keep the use of `!ok` to 100% avoid a nil value going into the switch statement lower down.

When ok == false it means the provider is already in the cache so it should be in the previous locks (so is redundant to checking for the returned value from AllProviders being non-nil), so there's redundancy here, but I'm not too fussed after all.
This line wasn't causing an issue ATM, but it looked like dead code (and the comment was misleading) so I removed it 🙂
I'm not sure why we weren't always returning diags here, this change just ensures we don't also return the unknown diagnostic below (which I noticed when writing my tests)

Looks like this fix might have triggered another test failure 👀:
```bash
--- FAIL: TestContext2Plan_importSelfReferenceInModule (0.00s)
    context_plan_import_test.go:1984: expected one diag, got 0: %!s(<nil>)
FAIL
```

Reading this fix back, it's incorrect for sure.... The import block edges need to be created using the module the block is defined in, not the target node which defines the references 🤔 

Back to the drawing board!
I fixed this in 79f78393e3cce27689db97a9267be2cbe1677bb1 , as I misunderstood what module context was being used for the references 😅
@mildwonkey you might have already seen, but this line addresses your comment in the other PR -> https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/pull/38993#discussion_r3775010333

@mildwonkey tagging you hoping you might have more context on whether this was the right fix (or if there might be other places to check for errors like this).

Originally I thought maybe `i.Config.ToResource` was incorrect and needed to be fixed, but I saw we recently added `i.AbsToConfigResource` and that made me think that `i.Config.ToResource` was kept to be relative purposefully 🤔

No, I suspect that was an oversight from before that field existed. Once we have an ImportStatement we should use the AbsToConfigResource - we shouldn't have to refer to the relative module outside of config loading (I'm pretty sure, at least!).

There's one other line you might want to check in this file, 278? It should also being using AbsToConfigResource. That's the only other use of that method outside of configs & refactoring (where the FindImportStatement method that adds that AbsToConfigResource lives)
I think this is the last one. Thanks for taking care of this!

Ah, good find. I actually ended up running into this one when writing a test for #39010, so that PR already has the [fix](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/pull/39010/changes#diff-eae4ab33ad5bab5fbde2fcc9be6715f9fb067a051d73d7256f520825a4f20daa) 👍🏻

I originally wrote this as `EmptyLiner` interface with an `EmptyLine` method, but I figured as interfaces should describe actions and the empty lines space things out... I landed on `Spacer`. Happy to hear alternatives if this name rubs people the wrong way.

human_labels.body:
A race was introduced here by this PR's other fix...

```diff
- r.renewDiags.Append(diags)
+ r.renewDiags = r.renewDiags.Append(diags)
```

...introducing a new write to the r.renewDiags field. The mutex addresses that.
These tests are super basic, but my hope is that in future when we can make the methods do the message formatting, not calling code, then these pre-existing tests only need to be updated then.
Also, it demonstrates how the new methods continue to log these as "log" type.

I think users might find the use of versions and version constraints next to each other a bit confusing if the constraint doesn't have an operator. That'd be on the user, as they'd be the person who set the constraint, but I could imagine someone being confused by `v2.0.0` versus `2.0.0` in these logs.

How much work would it be to enforce an operator being present? Do you think the benefit is worth the effort?
Love how disproportionately small the changed LOC is versus the pain to test this 😅

This test looks good to me, and I've been thinking about what it'd look like to test the unhappy path for an upgrade. The thing is, I believe that all unhappy paths are essentially the same in this command, so there isn't a special 'failing upgrade test' to write. We just want to know that the lock file is definitely not changed when an error occurs and a different provider or provider version was used for the destination store.

I don't think we have an integration test that forces an error during initialisation of the destination state store, and/or an error in the migration process itself. Could you please add one? That integration test wouldn't need to be specifically for an upgrade scenario, but it would equally cover us for a failure in an upgrade scenario (hopefully that makes sense). E.g. testing a failed migration to another provider and asserting that the lock file isn't changed to include the new provider would be equally applicable for a scenario where the failed migration was to a different provider _version_. But making an integration test for the first scenario is infinitely easier.
This was a great approach!
I think it's less of an issue in the context of output, compared to entry (declaring those in configuration) but I do agree it can still be confusing. I'll look into this.

> I don't think we have an integration test that forces an error during initialisation of the destination state store, and/or an error in the migration process itself. Could you please add one?

Sure 👍🏻
See https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/pull/38934
I'd be happy to add some more tests involving other commands but I think that could be done as part other PRs?

We discussed this privately via Slack, I'm just repeating the conclusions here for posterity:

If we are to enforce presence of the operator (= specifically) it would require us to re-implement the [String function](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/92c3ab2f3108cce9c2cb942e0b843d23b5899bba/internal/getproviders/types.go#L360-L362) and/or modify [the underlying implementation which intentionally omits it](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/92c3ab2f3108cce9c2cb942e0b843d23b5899bba/internal/getproviders/providerreqs/version.go#L201-L202).

I’m leaning towards keeping that as-is because it either falls under high-risk low-reward category (changing a lot of other outputs), or messy implementation (having two functions that render the same thing differently depending on context).

I was imagining a test for just the `state migrate` command, where we show that an error in either destination backend initialisation OR the migration process itself (you could do just one) doesn't result in changes to the lock file. I'm not sure why https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/pull/38934 or tests for other commands besides `state migrate` are related to my comment?

I was imagining a single integration test being added. If that's in a separate PR that's fine.

I can add that, I may have misinterpreted this part of your earlier comment

> That integration test wouldn't need to be specifically for an upgrade scenario, but it would equally cover us for a failure in an upgrade scenario

I thought it was a bit confusing as well 😀 glad we cleared it out
Added a test in 075860f3d6aaf598df639bbb9fa1a137e65b2810

human_labels.body:
```suggestion
body: "version: JSON output now includes a new `format_version` field, which will enable safer future changes of the command's JSON output format. It is assumed existing tooling ignores unknown fields and therefore this change should not be breaking in itself but we advice consumers to pay attention to `format_version` in future releases and/or use latest version of hashicorp/terraform-json & hashicorp/terraform-exec which does."
```

A few points:

 - We cannot assume all consuming programs are in Go, so the wording should not assume that either.
 - I think we should update (and release) the libraries before merging this and that way we can avoid "promises" in the Changelog.
(just thinking out loud) I assume the consumer side of this will likely have `omitempty` but of course that's not important here on the producer side.

Also, I would avoid saying this `format_version` "enables extension with new fields" because in the past we have considered that as a non-breaking change. It is still usually reflected in the `format_version` but only as minor bump and we assume that bump to be more advisory (e.g. to nudge consumers to log that as "WARN" somewhere but not to prevent them from parsing the rest of the output).

The versioning crucially allows us to modify existing fields or remove fields - which are breaking changes and would necessitate bumping the major version.

In future we could revise this approach: e.g. we could instead make upgrade of the PSS provider get skipped in getProviders, instead of allowing upgrade to happen but not enter the lock file.

But for now, this change makes what's happening more explicit. Before, `saveDependencyLockFile` was merging locks internally in a way that happened to stop upgraded locks for the PSS provider being persisted in the file. I've pulled that merging up and out of the method to here, made it conditional, and added code comments so it's more transparent what's happening.


So if:
- PSS is not in use:  the locks saved to disk are all the ones described in config/state that are returned from `getProviders`
- PSS is in use: the lock from `getProvidersFromPSSConfig` is used, and all locks for other providers returned from `getProviders` are added to that single lock. This is saved to disk, so the PSS provider lock from `getProvidersFromPSSConfig` is overridden. In an upgrade scenario the overridden lock might be for a newer version.

I'm a bit confused about this check here. How can we make assumptions about this being user-supplied vs not? I mean - what if the user supplied that exact value? Also why is relative path to the same file (e.g. `-state-provider-lock-file=.terraform.lock.hcl`) treated differently to an absolute one (e.g. `-state-provider-lock-file=$(pwd)/.terraform.lock.hcl`)?

I don't know the exact right wording but just noting for our discussion later that we should at least attempt to find a more "actionable" one than this

> Please ensure the lock file contains a lock for the state store provider and try again.

I think the user could benefit from knowing what to do (i.e. _how_ to do it), not just that it needs to be done.
Perhaps worth a separate commit but I think the `maps.Values()` here is unnecessary.
